home.kicker: NASA Space Apps · Make wildfire data easier to use
home.title: Is this fire season normal?
home.lead: NIRAN compares each month's satellite fire detections with the same month in other years, then says it in one sentence.
how: The word and the colour give the month's verdict.
The curve shows whether the year left its usual range.
The bars set this month against the other years.
home.usualNote: Usual level: median of the same period in the other years ({first}–{last}), summed across countries.

method.title: Method and sources
method.intro: Where NIRAN's numbers come from, what we removed, how a month gets its level, and what the data cannot tell you.

sections.title: Where the data comes from
body: Fire detections come from NASA FIRMS. The MODIS instrument on the Terra and Aqua satellites spots unusually hot points on the ground several times a day, in pixels about 1 km wide.
We use the 2020–2024 FIRMS archive for Morocco, Australia and Brazil. Weather comes from NASA POWER, land cover from the MODIS MCD12Q1 product served by NASA GIBS, and open wildfires from NASA EONET.

sections.title: What we removed
body: We keep presumed vegetation fires only: volcanoes, fixed heat sources (factories, gas flares) and offshore detections are dropped.
We drop low-confidence detections (MODIS confidence below 30%).
We drop places that 'burn' more than 60 days a year for several years: those are industrial sites, not fires.

sections.title: How a month gets its level
body: Each month is compared with the same month in the other years, in the same country: July 2022 against the other Julys. The fire season is built in.
The year being tested is left out of its own comparison, so an extreme month cannot hide itself.
The usual level is the median, the middle value, which one wild year cannot drag. The further a month sits from it, the higher its level:
after: Safeguard: where fires are rare (fewer than 5 a month), a country stays 'normal'. Three fires instead of one is not an alert.

sections.title: Conditions and land cover
body: Temperature and rain are NASA POWER monthly values at the four busiest fire areas of each country, compared with the same month over 2001–2024.
'What burned' places every detection on the MODIS land cover map of its year: forest, shrub and savanna, cropland or other.
These are conditions seen at the time, not proof of a cause: most fires are lit by people.

sections.title: Limits
body: A detection is not a burned area: a large fire can make hundreds of detections, a small one none.
Clouds and thick smoke hide fires, and the satellites pass only a few times a day, so short fires can be missed.
Small farm fires often fall below what MODIS can see.
The FIRMS history here covers 2020–2024, so each month is compared with only 4 other years. The usual level is still fragile.
The satellite orbits on the globe are drawn to explain how MODIS scans; they are not live positions.
